pr_body:
The cache maintains a list of all regexes in the cache, which it uses to be able to randomly access members as part of evicting when the cache is full and an item needs to be replaced. When evicting, it randomly samples a subset of the items, and then removes whichever is found to have the oldest timestamp. That RemoveAt call is O(N), as elements need to be shifted down. But the order of the list doesn't actually matter, so we can make that instead be O(1) by just moving the last element into the removal slot (overwriting the one to be removed) and then shrinking the size of the list.

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/106346

> thoughts on these 2 cases? Appear to be Linux only.

Hi @steveharter , just have a look at it and find following:

these 2 cases are about `[Arguments(40_000, 1_600, 800)]` so which means unique regexps size > cache size (so will trigger cache expulsion) and cache size > `MaxExamineOnDrop` (so RegexCache will use [random](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/67df47e1abb45b08f32063737e1e0f6eecb083e7/src/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/src/System/Text/RegularExpressions/Regex.Cache.cs#L224) subset to do cache expulsion). 

Consider this test case also uses [random](https://github.com/dotnet/performance/blob/288a0263260988ab379f4e129ea5e2fb28c38b72/src/benchmarks/micro/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/Perf.Regex.Cache.cs#L108) regexp generation orders, so I feel improved LRU of RegexCache cannot give benefit for it.

For regression of these cases, I cannot find obvious reason with #105746 by now. The different behaviors I can find for these cases is: when RegexCache needs to expel 'oldest' item, previous code can skip some [integer values exchange](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/67df47e1abb45b08f32063737e1e0f6eecb083e7/src/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/src/System/Text/RegularExpressions/Regex.Cache.cs#L244) and timestamp for all cache items can keep low value (0, 1 maybe ) which were because all new coming regexps had timestamp value of 0, which causes subsequent regexp request (even if requested regexp was in cache and had high timestamp) resets its timestamp [back to 0 + 1](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/67df47e1abb45b08f32063737e1e0f6eecb083e7/src/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/src/System/Text/RegularExpressions/Regex.Cache.cs#L182). Isn't this behavior unexpected ? Beside of these, I haven't found other difference in RegexCache level :(

> which causes subsequent regexp request (even if requested regexp was in cache and had high timestamp) resets its timestamp back to 0 + 1. Isn't this behavior unexpected?

I don't see how the subsequent node is reset it back to 0 + 1 - only a new node (with the fix in the recent PR) and cache hits do the lastAccessedStamp + 1. The LRU doesn't favor how many times a given node was accessed; every time there is a different node being requested, it will be given priority (+1) over the previously used one.

For the given test parameters, there will be very few cache hits so perhaps the extra field set + `Volatile.Read` added by the PR would be the cause, although a perf diff of ~30% seems a bit out of balance. Perhaps Linux is super slow on field writes\reads, or slow due to the referencing of s_lastAccessed across the 4 threads as the test configures, or there was a recent regression around field access.

In either case, the test is really verifying the cache algorithm isn't O(n2), which it isn't, so the perf diff is not all that critical.

> I don't see how the subsequent node is reset it back to 0 + 1 - only a new node (with the fix in the recent PR) and cache hits do the lastAccessedStamp + 1.

@steveharter  `reset it back to '0 + 1'` - I mean this will be caused by previous code before recent PR. As you said, this test case will have very few cache hits so "a new node comes" may easily happen. For previous code, new node will be treated as `lastNode` BUT with timestamp 0 . So later when a existing cache node hits (say its timestamp was 5), it will be reset back to '0 + 1' because its updated timestamp value is calculated like `lastNode.Timestamp + 1`

> The LRU doesn't favor how many times a given node was accessed; every time there is a different node being requested, it will be given priority (+1) over the previously used one.

Agree. I mean previous code breaks this expectation, at least last requested 'existing' cache node may be changed back from '5' to '1' as explained above, and last requested 'new' node had least priority 0. 

These are why I guess the specified test cases run by previous code will make lots of low timestamp values (0 or 1...). However I am not sure it is the regression reason, just provide one different behavior between before and after fix PR.

When a new node is added to the cache, it's added at the end of the list. Previously it was being added with a really low timestamp, now it's not (which is the bug fix).

When we go to evict an entry from the cache, we randomly sample the entries and remove whichever we see with the lowest timestamp. Some percentage of the time, that lowest one would have been the newly added one. Removing is an O(N) `List<T>.RemoveAt`, but the closer to the end of the list that removal is, the cheaper it will be: if it's the last item, it's O(1). The way the test is set up, we're now likely to end up removing an item from the list with a small index, making the removal closer to O(N). But, we don't examine the full list, we only examine a max of 30, so in this test that's got a cache size of 800, we're only examining 30 / 800 items each eviction, and so on average we'll only include the newest one ~4% of the time. So it's increased the cost of ~4% from O(1) to O(N).

review_comments:
"shift up" instead of "shift down"?

In either case, this makes sense to avoid the perf hit of the copy\shift during Remove().
Shift down, e.g. removing element 0 means moving elements 1 through N to be 0 through N-1.
